name: Joseph P. Kennedy Sr.
role: First SEC chairman (1934-35), first Maritime Commission chairman (1937-38), U.S. ambassador to Britain (1938-40)
summary: As SEC chairman, Kennedy oversaw the introduction of securities registration and disclosure rules. He advocated aid to Britain while opposing American entry into the European war before an attack on the United States. In 1950 he urged withdrawal from Korea and other positions peripheral to American defence, and argued that the United States should coexist with communist governments overseas.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Under Kennedy the SEC adopted permanent securities registration forms and promulgated ownership reporting forms for corporate officers, directors and large shareholders. It published monthly summaries of those filings.

reviewHistory.rationale: As SEC chairman he said the regulation of the investment market 'must be apparent to all right-thinking people', that 'we cannot turn back', and that for dishonest promoters the rules 'can't be too strict'; he backed disclosure and supervision of corporations, while stressing honest business had nothing to fear.

strong-leader.rationale: Kennedy supported giving officials powers adequate to their responsibilities and argued that the emergency did not justify the proposed transfer of congressional authority. The address does not say whether a leader should be able to bypass political deadlock.

reviewHistory.rationale: Mixed: in January 1941 he said he was 'a great believer in centralized responsibility', yet opposed the Lend-Lease bill as a surrender of Congress's authority to the executive.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Kennedy argued that the United Nations should serve as a forum and provide for voluntary cooperation. He rejected the idea that it could function as a governing body compelling compliance across blocs.

nation-first.rationale: Kennedy made the interests of the United States his test for aid and entry into war in 1941. In 1950 he again gave American security and economic strength priority over maintaining international commitments.

reviewHistory.rationale: In 1941 he said the test of any proposal should be 'what is best for the United States of America'; in 1950 he urged leaving Asian commitments the U.S. would not defend for its own sake.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: During the Algic sit-down strike in Montevideo, Kennedy ordered striking crew members put in irons. His commission also formally recommended remedial maritime legislation after the incident.

reviewHistory.rationale: Contested and narrow: the Commission he chaired condemned sit-down and quickie strikes on ships and recommended remedial legislation after the Algic incident, and a union biography reports he pushed to outlaw maritime strikes; this concerns seamen only and secret ballots are not mentioned.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Kennedy sought to abandon overextended commitments in Europe and Asia while calling for defence cooperation in the Western Hemisphere. His speech does not specify whether that cooperation could take the form of a permanent alliance.

reviewHistory.rationale: In December 1950 he called for getting out of Korea and every point in Asia not needed for U.S. defence, then applying 'the same principle in Europe', including ending support for Chiang and the French in Indochina (as reported by Nasaw via The Nation).

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Kennedy backed a grant to Britain and argued against overseas commitments that exceeded American resources. He did not address a duty to provide substantial aid to poor people wherever they live.

defeat-communism.rationale: Kennedy urged the United States to let communist rule in Europe and Asia run its course and to deter attacks on its own hemisphere. He argued that the two sides had to coexist and that military containment had reinforced communist unity.

reviewHistory.rationale: In 1947 he argued the U.S. should 'permit communism outside the Soviet Union to have its trial' and in 1950 that negotiating with the Soviets was not weakness; he judged Communism harmful but not to be fought abroad.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Kennedy criticized military aid to North Atlantic Pact countries and urged abandoning the attempt to hold a line in continental Europe. He left open conditional help to European governments and did not explicitly say the United States should leave the pact or stay out of military blocs.

reviewHistory.rationale: In 1950 he held that Communist rule abroad was not a threat to U.S. security and proposed withdrawing from Asia and Europe; earlier he supported neutrality after 1939 and urged staying out of the European war.

military-force-for-human-rights.rationale: In 1950 Kennedy argued for intervention only where American interests and homes were threatened and opposed using force to sustain preferred governments in Asia.

foreign-policy-non-interference.rationale: Kennedy called for leaving other countries to manage their own affairs and making an exception when American interests and homes were threatened. He held up intervention in Italian elections and support for French rule in Indochina as examples of overreach.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Kennedy proposed ending US military commitments unrelated to American defence and choosing where to fight by what was necessary to defend the country. His 1941 address likewise opposed entering the European war unless the United States was attacked.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: Kennedy opposed making political systems overseas an American responsibility. He criticized American intervention in Italian elections and argued against intervention to realize Syngman Rhee’s model of democracy in Korea.
